855.title: What people live by
855.hook: in Tolstoy's story an angel learns that people live by love (What Men Live By)
855.howItsDone: Tolstoy's short story What Men Live By is a moral tale; readers take from it the angel's three answers: love dwells in people, no one knows their own needs, and people live by love.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Simone Weil, who called attention the rarest and purest form of generosity. Your line was what they are going through. Today, a story about a stranger who needed far more than five minutes.

Winter, in a Russian village. A poor shoemaker named Simon is walking home with no sheepskin, because the people who owed him money didn't pay. Behind a roadside shrine he sees something pale: a man, naked, sitting against the wall, freezing. Simon is frightened. He walks right past. Then, a little way down the road, he stops, argues with himself, and turns back. That turn begins a short story by Leo Tolstoy called What Men Live By.
screen: `A POOR SHOEMAKER IN WINTER.` → `A MAN BEHIND THE SHRINE.` → `SIMON TURNS BACK.`

segments.voice: Simon gives the man his coat and brings him home. His wife Matryona is furious: no sheepskin, and now another mouth to feed. Then she looks at the stranger, and pity wins. She sets out bread, and the stranger, for the first time, smiles. He gives his name as Michael, and stays on, learning to make shoes. One day a wealthy gentleman storms in and orders boots that must last a year without losing their shape. As he gives the order, Michael looks past him and smiles a second time. Then Michael makes soft slippers instead. Simon is horrified, until a servant runs back: the master has died on the way home, and they need slippers for the body. Later a woman comes in with twin girls, one of them lame. Their mother died when they were born, and this neighbor took them in and raised them as her own. Michael smiles a third time. Then he reveals that he is an angel. He was sent to take the twins' mother's soul and refused out of pity, so he was sent to earth to learn three things. What dwells in people: love. What isn't given to people: to know their own needs, even what they'll need by evening. And what people live by. Not by careful planning for themselves, the angel says, but by love.
screen: `A STRANGER AT THE TABLE.` · `BOOTS FOR A YEAR, SLIPPERS FOR A BODY.` · `TWIN GIRLS, RAISED BY A NEIGHBOR.` · `THE THREE ANSWERS.` · then, large: `PEOPLE LIVE BY LOVE.`

segments.voice: The twins lived because someone who didn't have to took them in; look back over your own life the same way. Who fed you, taught you, drove you, sat up with you when you were sick? Let the names and faces come one at a time, family and maybe a surprise or two, a teacher, a neighbor, a stranger at the right moment, and if you pray, give thanks in your own tradition's words.
Michael. The angel in Tolstoy's story who learns, through a shoemaker's family, that people live not by planning but by love. Today's word.
Your line: what we live by. Three smiles, three answers. Day eight hundred fifty-five, done.

856.title: Goodwill for all
856.hook: Martin Luther King Jr. described agape as understanding, redeeming goodwill for all (Stride Toward Freedom)
856.howItsDone: In the nonviolent tradition Martin Luther King Jr. described, participants commit to opposing unjust deeds while seeking the good of their opponents, aiming at reconciliation rather than humiliation.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Michael, Tolstoy's angel, who learned that people live by love. Your line was what we live by. Today, love aimed at a hard target.

Black residents of Montgomery, Alabama, have stopped riding the city buses. Day after day they walk to work, in the cold and the rain. Their homes are threatened. Their leaders are arrested. One of those leaders, a minister named Martin Luther King Jr., faces a hard question: how should the people feel about the ones doing this to them? Later, in a book about those days called Stride Toward Freedom, he gave his answer. He reached for an old Greek word for love, and gave it a definition.
screen: `MONTGOMERY, ALABAMA.` → `WALKING, NOT RIDING.` → `HOW TO FEEL ABOUT OPPONENTS?`

segments.voice: King lays out three Greek words. Eros, a longing, even a love of beauty. Philia, the warm love between friends, who love each other back. And agape, the one he means. King describes agape as understanding, redeeming goodwill for all people. It doesn't wait to be earned, and it doesn't ask anything back. It isn't liking: nobody is being asked to feel affection for the person who bombed their house. Agape is a settled will for the other person's good. King writes that agape loves the person who does an evil deed while hating the deed itself. That's what made his kind of nonviolence different from simply staying quiet. The boycott kept pushing. The goal, he says, was not to defeat or humiliate opponents, but to win their friendship and understanding. King, a Baptist minister, rooted this in the Gospels, and he credited Gandhi with showing him the method. In the King James Bible, Jesus says: "Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you." King's agape is that command, worked out in the streets of a real city, with real people on the other side.
screen: `THREE WORDS FOR LOVE.` · `UNDERSTANDING, REDEEMING GOODWILL.` · `THE PERSON, NOT THE DEED.` · `LOVE YOUR ENEMIES.` · then, large: `GOODWILL FOR ALL.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you're at odds with, not the hardest person in your life, someone medium: a coworker, a relative, a neighbor whose politics drive you up the wall. You don't have to like them; just try King's distinction, set the deed to one side and look at the person, and without forcing a feeling, hold one simple wish for their good, that they're well, that they're understood. If prayer is part of your life, let the wish go there too.
Agape. Martin Luther King Jr.'s word for understanding, redeeming goodwill for all people, even those who do you harm. Today's word.
Your line: win their friendship and understanding. Agape aims at the person's good, never their humiliation. That's day eight hundred fifty-six.

857.title: It grows
857.hook: a study tested whether weeks of loving-kindness practice change a person's days
857.howItsDone: Buddhist meditators practice loving-kindness (metta) by silently wishing well to themselves and others in widening circles, often for a set time each day; the practice is also taught in secular meditation courses and has been studied by psychologists.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was agape: understanding, redeeming goodwill for all, as Martin Luther King Jr. described it. Your line was win their friendship and understanding.

May all beings be happy. That's the heart of an old Buddhist teaching, the Metta Sutta, which describes a love meant to reach every living thing, near and far, seen and unseen. Say a sentence like that, and a fair question comes up. Does saying it change anything in the one who says it? A team of psychologists decided to find out. They taught a group of working adults a loving-kindness meditation, then followed them week after week, asking each evening how the day had gone inside.
screen: `MAY ALL BEINGS BE HAPPY.` → `DOES SAYING IT CHANGE ANYTHING?` → `A TEAM DECIDED TO FIND OUT.`

segments.voice: First, a practice, not a mood. The Metta Sutta speaks of cultivating a boundless heart toward all beings, the way a mother guards her only child. Buddhist teachers call metta a practice: you bring someone to mind and wish them well on purpose, whether or not the warmth shows up. Second, the study. Psychologist Barbara Fredrickson and her colleagues ran it. Some participants learned loving-kindness meditation; a comparison group waited their turn for the course. Both kept reporting on their days. Over the weeks, the meditators reported more positive emotions in ordinary life: joy, gratitude, contentment, hope and love. Third, small days, stacked up. The gains didn't arrive on day one. The paper describes them showing up gradually, as people kept practicing. Nobody flipped a switch. Something got watered. Fourth, what it built. Fredrickson's larger idea is called broaden and build: good feelings widen what a person notices, and over time they build lasting resources. The meditators also reported more sense of purpose, more support from others, and more satisfaction with their lives. Now the honest part. This is one study. People reported on themselves, and the changes were modest. It proves nothing about the deep nature of love. But on one plain point it agrees with the old sutta: this kind of love is something a person can grow.
screen: `A PRACTICE, NOT A MOOD.` · `THE STUDY: WEEKS, NOT MOMENTS.` · `SMALL DAYS, STACKED UP.` · `WHAT IT BUILT.` · then, large: `IT GROWS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone easy to love, a friend, a grandparent, a pet, and silently offer them the kind of wish the practice uses: may you be well, may you be at ease. Stay with this one person, repeating the wish at the pace of the breath; if warmth comes, fine, and if it doesn't, keep going anyway, the way a gardener waters the same bed every day. If you pray, you can hold them before God as you go.
It grows. Loving-kindness treated as a practice that strengthens with use, as the Metta Sutta teaches and a modern study set out to test. Today's word.
Your line: something got watered. Love like this is grown, a little at a time. Day eight hundred fifty-seven, done.

858.title: The difficult
858.hook: love isn't only for the easy ones
858.howItsDone: In Buddhist loving-kindness practice, people often wish well to themselves, a friend and a neutral person before turning to someone difficult; Jews and Christians read Proverbs 25 on feeding a hungry enemy as practical guidance; Stoics prepare in the morning for the people they will meet.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was it grows: loving-kindness, strengthened by practice. Your line was something got watered.

"Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busy-body, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial." That's how a Roman emperor, Marcus Aurelius, opens the second book of his private notebook. Not a pep talk. A weather report. He ran an empire, and he knew the day would include people who were hard to be around. So do the rest of us: a coworker who takes credit, a relative who knows exactly which button to press, a neighbor with a leaf blower and opinions. Loving the easy ones takes no training at all.
screen: `BEGIN THE MORNING BY SAYING TO THYSELF.` → `A WEATHER REPORT.` → `THE OTHER ONES.`

segments.voice: First, the emperor's warning. Marcus goes on: these people act as they do because they don't know what is good and bad. None of them can make him do wrong, so none of them can really injure him, and he can't hate them, because they are his kin. Then, surprising for an emperor: we are made for cooperation, like feet, like hands, like eyelids. To work against each other is against nature. Second, bread for an enemy. The book of Proverbs puts it in kitchen terms: "If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat; and if he be thirsty, give him water to drink." Nothing about warm feelings. Bread and water, handed to someone who wishes you harm. Third, the hard one comes last. In the Path of Purification, the Buddhist teacher Buddhaghosa gives an order for loving-kindness practice: yourself, then a dear friend, then someone neutral, and only then someone hostile. He warns against starting with the hostile person, because resentment comes up first. He doesn't pretend it's easy; he builds a ramp. Fourth, well-wishing isn't trusting. None of these voices asks anyone to hand a difficult person the car keys. Wishing someone well can sit alongside a locked door, a firm no, a boundary kept: hoping they find their way to being well, from a safe distance if need be. The hard ones too. Not first, not instead of safety, but too.
screen: `THE EMPEROR'S MORNING WARNING.` · `BREAD FOR AN ENEMY.` · `THE HARD ONE COMES LAST.` · `WELL-WISHING ISN'T TRUSTING.` · then, large: `THE HARD ONES TOO.`

segments.voice: Walk Buddhaghosa's ramp slowly: may I be well, then a friend for a few breaths, then a neutral face from the store, and only then someone mildly difficult, a person who simply irritates you, offered the same wish. If resentment comes up, go back to the friend for a breath and try again. If you pray, you can name them before God.
The difficult. The people who are hard to love, whom Marcus expected each morning, Proverbs says to feed anyway, and Buddhaghosa placed last on the ramp. Today's word.
Your line: the hard ones too. Bread and water count, even when the warmth is missing. See you tomorrow.

859.title: Your own body
859.hook: several traditions honor the body as gift or temple
859.howItsDone: Some Christians speak of the body as a temple, after Paul's letter to the Corinthians; Jews and Christians pray the Psalms, including the praise of being wonderfully made; Buddhists tell how the Buddha left behind extreme fasting and took food before his awakening.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the difficult: people hard to love, wished well anyway. Your line was the hard ones too.

Knees that click on the stairs. A back that votes against getting out of bed. A face under the bathroom light at seven in the morning. For some people, the harshest words of the whole day are said silently, to their own body. Meanwhile that same body has been breathing all night without being asked, healing a paper cut nobody thanked it for, and carrying its owner to the mirror to be criticized. This stretch of the path is about love. Today it turns to the one thing every listener is living in.
screen: `KNEES THAT CLICK ON THE STAIRS.` → `WORDS SAID SILENTLY TO A BODY.` → `BREATHING ALL NIGHT, UNTHANKED.`

segments.voice: First, fearfully and wonderfully made. In the Psalms, a singer looks at their own body and starts praising: "I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made." Not perfectly made, not admired by others. Wonderfully, with a little awe mixed in. The body is a gift and a wonder before it's anything else. Second, a temple, not a project. Writing to Christians in Corinth who were arguing about what they could do with their bodies, Paul asks: "know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you". In context he's warning them about how they use their bodies, and the image raises the stakes: a temple is holy, a place where God dwells, not something to use carelessly. Third, the Buddha accepts a meal. In a sutta in the Middle Length Discourses, the Buddha remembers his life before awakening. He tried to wring freedom out of his body by starving it, until it was skin and bone. It didn't work. Then he remembered sitting peacefully under a tree as a boy, and asked whether that kind of ease was really something to fear. He decided it wasn't, and took solid food again. The way forward began with a meal. Fourth, kind, not perfect. None of these texts asks for a body that looks a certain way. They ask for something smaller: reverence, care, an end to treating it as an enemy. Sleep when it's tired. Feed it. This body, as it is.
screen: `FEARFULLY AND WONDERFULLY MADE.` · `A TEMPLE, NOT A PROJECT.` · `THE BUDDHA ACCEPTS A MEAL.` · `KIND, NOT PERFECT.` · then, large: `THIS BODY.`

segments.voice: Sit or lie down, whatever is kind to your back, and move your attention slowly from the feet upward, legs, belly, hands, shoulders, face, silently thanking each part for today. Wherever there's an ache, rest there for a breath the way you'd sit with a tired friend, and if the old critical words show up, let them pass and go back to thanks. If you pray, you can give thanks to God for this body.
Temple. Paul's word for the body: a place where God dwells, to be cared for, not used carelessly. Today's word.
Your line: this body. It has been carrying you all along. That's day eight hundred fifty-nine.

860.title: Loving a partner
860.hook: love as daily choice, not only feeling
860.howItsDone: Jews and Christians read the Song of Songs as a love poem and as a picture of love between God and people; Christians read Paul's words on love in 1 Corinthians 13, sometimes at weddings; some couples, religious or not, describe their commitment as something renewed in small daily acts.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was temple: Paul's word for the body, holy and worth care. Your line was this body.

English has a strange phrase for the start of love. People fall into it. Falling is something that happens to you: no plan, no effort, just gravity. That's a fine way to begin. But nobody falls into doing the dishes at eleven at night so the other person can sleep, or into listening to the same work story for the third time with real interest. Those things are done on purpose, on ordinary days, when the feeling is quiet. So what is love once the falling is over?
screen: `PEOPLE FALL INTO IT.` → `NOBODY FALLS INTO THE DISHES.` → `ONCE THE FALLING IS OVER.`

segments.voice: First, the song. The Song of Songs in the Hebrew Bible is a long love poem, full of gardens and longing, and near its end it says: "Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it." Some Jewish and Christian readers take the Song as a picture of love between God and people; others read it as a song about two lovers. Either way, the claim is about endurance. Second, the letter. Paul, writing to the church in Corinth, describes love in the King James wording as charity: "Charity suffereth long, and is kind." Notice the verbs: suffering long, being kind, not envying. Paul isn't describing a feeling that washes over someone; he's describing how a person behaves, especially when it's hard. Third, the book. The psychoanalyst Erich Fromm, in The Art of Loving, argued that love is an art, learned and practiced, and that loving someone is more than a strong feeling. He called it a decision, a judgment and a promise. A feeling can come and go; a promise can be kept on the days the feeling is away. Fourth, small choices, daily. None of these voices says feelings don't matter, only that they aren't the whole of it. Love between partners lives in small acts: a coffee made the way the other person likes it, a phone put face down, an apology offered first. And choosing love daily never means choosing to stay where you're harmed. A daily choice is made freely, by both.
screen: `MANY WATERS CANNOT QUENCH LOVE.` · `CHARITY SUFFERETH LONG.` · `A DECISION, A PROMISE.` · `SMALL CHOICES, DAILY.` · then, large: `A DAILY CHOICE.`

segments.voice: Let a partner come to mind, or, if there isn't one right now, anyone you've decided to love: a sibling, a close friend, a parent. Holding their face, ask quietly what small thing, not a grand gesture, would make their day a little lighter, and let one answer settle while you simply wish them well. If you pray, you can hold them before God by name.
Erich Fromm. The psychoanalyst who called love a decision, a judgment and a promise, something practiced like an art. Today's word.
Your line: a daily choice. The falling was the start; the choosing is the rest. Until tomorrow.

861.title: Friendship kept up
861.howItsDone: In Jewish and Christian tradition, Proverbs is read as practical wisdom about friendship; people keep friendships alive through visits, calls, letters and shared meals, sometimes around holidays and life events.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Erich Fromm, who called love a decision, a judgment and a promise. Your line was a daily choice.

Somewhere in a phone there's a name that used to be a daily call. Nobody fought. Nobody decided anything. One of you moved, or had a baby, or changed jobs, and the calls became texts, the texts became birthday messages, and then one year even the birthday slipped by. Sometimes a friendship ends like a houseplant on a high shelf: not killed, just not watered. Marriages have vows and anniversaries. Families have holidays. Friendship mostly has nothing holding it up except the people in it.
screen: `A NAME THAT USED TO BE A DAILY CALL.` → `NOBODY DECIDED ANYTHING.` → `A HOUSEPLANT ON A HIGH SHELF.`

segments.voice: First, Proverbs on the old friend: "Thine own friend, and thy father's friend, forsake not." Look at the second half: not just your friend, but your father's friend, someone you inherited. Proverbs treats an old friendship as worth keeping across a lifetime, even passed down like a family table. Second, shew himself friendly. Another proverb, in the King James wording: "A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly." Having friends and showing friendliness are tied together. The friendship doesn't run on its own; someone has to keep showing up. Third, to have a friend, be one. Ralph Waldo Emerson, in his essay on friendship, puts it in one line: "The only way to have a friend is to be one." Emerson can be lofty about friendship, but this line is practical. It moves the question from whether they've called lately to whether you have. Fourth, small, often, on purpose. Tending a friendship isn't a big reunion trip. It's a short message that says I thought of you, a photo of the café you both used to sit in, a question about their mother's surgery. And look back at the week, which has been love in practice: what we live by, win their friendship and understanding, something got watered, the hard ones too, this body, a daily choice, and now tend it. Each one moved love from a feeling toward something done.
screen: `FORSAKE NOT YOUR FATHER'S FRIEND.` · `SHEW HIMSELF FRIENDLY.` · `TO HAVE A FRIEND, BE ONE.` · `SMALL, OFTEN, ON PURPOSE.` · then, large: `TEND IT.`

segments.voice: Let a friend come to mind whom you haven't spoken to in a while, not someone who hurt you, just someone the current carried away, and stay with one specific moment you shared: a joke, a kitchen, a long drive. Then turn Emerson's line around on yourself, and let one short, light message take shape in your mind, the kind that simply says they came to mind. If you pray, you can give thanks for them by name.
Emerson. The essayist who wrote that the only way to have a friend is to be one. Today's word.
Your line: tend it. A friendship is kept the way a plant is, with a little water, often. Day eight hundred sixty-one, done.
